implementation_notes: Default for async programs: the sender is the hub (clone it per publisher), Sender::subscribe() is the subscription API, and the bounded capacity plus RecvError::Lagged give an explicit overflow story instead of an unbounded queue. Requires a tokio runtime for recv().await; the same crate also backs the multi-consumer pattern where a receiver is wrapped in a task that republishes to application handlers.
pitfalls: recv() must handle RecvError::Lagged or subscribers silently lose events while the loop spins on Ok.
Sending fails with SendError when all receivers have been dropped, so publish results must be checked if the hub is supposed to outlive its subscribers.

variants.name: Synchronous Arc<dyn Fn> registry behind a Mutex
variants.idiom_name: Mutex<Vec<Arc<dyn Fn(&Event) + Send + Sync>>> + snapshot publish
variants.implementation_notes: Library-free realization for synchronous code: the hub is a struct owning a Mutex-guarded vector of Arc'd closures, subscribe pushes, publish clones the vector under the lock and then calls every handler outside it, which makes handlers that subscribe or unsubscribe during dispatch well-defined. Choose it when no async runtime is present, when delivery must be synchronous and ordered, or when events are cheap and the extra channel machinery of broadcast is not wanted.
pitfalls: Calling a handler while holding the Mutex deadlocks as soon as that handler subscribes or unsubscribes - always publish from a snapshot taken outside the lock.
Storing Arc<dyn Fn> keeps captured state alive forever; subscribers wanting automatic removal must key their entries and remove them on drop instead.
A panicking handler unwinds through the publish loop unless it is caught, so one bad subscriber can take down the publisher.
